final:
Everyone assumes fast food got expensive for the same reason everything else did — inflation, wages, supply chain chaos. The data suggests the story is more complicated than that. But a fast-food combo meal rose more than 100% between 2014 and 2024, outpacing gasoline, movie tickets, and median hourly wages over that same period.

That's not an inflation story. So where did the rest of that increase actually come from?

You used to be able to pull through a drive-through and grab a combo meal for under six dollars. That was 2014. Today, that same order — same restaurant, same basic meal — runs somewhere around twelve dollars. A published price comparison tracking fast-food combos across a decade found the increase lands at roughly $6.50, or more than 100%, between 2014 and 2024. Your pay went up. The burger went up faster.

The specifics are harder to dismiss than the average. A McDonald's Quarter Pounder with cheese meal sat at $5.39 in 2014. By 2024, the same item had reached $11.99 at McDonald's locations tracked in consumer reporting — more than doubling at a single chain. And McDonald's is not an outlier. Visual Capitalist's analysis of ten major fast-food chains found an average price increase of 63% over that decade, with McDonald's up 100%. These are not premium restaurants that quietly repositioned themselves upmarket. These are the places built around the promise of cheap, fast, and consistent.

Consumers registered the shift clearly. A Harris Poll found that 81% of adults who order from fast-food restaurants at least once a year said prices were higher than the year before — and only 32% agreed that quick-service restaurants still offer affordable meal options.

The commodity story starts with something real. Beginning in 2021, the prices restaurants paid for beef, chicken, and cooking oil each climbed into double-digit percentage increases from their 2020 baselines — not a gradual drift but a sharp, compressed run-up that lasted into 2023. Restaurants felt it in their costs.

What happened next followed a documented pattern. The repricing, when it came, was partial. A restaurant-cost analysis found that a one-percent rise in supply costs translated into roughly a 0.33% increase in cost of goods at constant menu prices, meaning the full shock never landed on the customer at once. It moved through the supply chain in fractions.

By 2022, a restaurant cost inflation survey found operators were reporting costs up 11.7% year over year, with raw materials and labor leading the increases. That's a genuine squeeze on businesses running tight margins, and it produced genuine price increases at the counter.

But National Restaurant Association models attributed only a minority of overall QSR menu-price growth to those commodity shocks. The input costs explain a real slice of what happened between 2019 and 2024. They do not explain most of it. Which raises the question the commodity story alone was never going to answer: where did the rest of the increase come from?

The industry's answer to all of this is straightforward, and it starts with real numbers. According to the National Restaurant Association, food costs for the average restaurant rose 35% over the five years following February 2020. Labor costs rose 35% over that same span. Menu prices, by the Association's own measure, increased 31% across that period — meaning the average operator was absorbing more in costs than they recovered at the counter.

The restaurant industry typically operates on slim margins of 3% to 5%. On a business running that thin, a simultaneous rise of roughly 35% on two of your three largest cost lines does not leave room to wait and see.

The cost structure itself explains why the pressure hits so hard. National Restaurant Association benchmarking data places quick-service restaurant costs at roughly 30% labor, 30% food and commodity inputs, and 25% occupancy. That means food and labor together account for roughly 60% of what it costs to run the kitchen before rent, insurance, or equipment enters the equation. When both of those lines move 35% in the same direction at the same time, the arithmetic compresses fast.

So the industry's explanation is not invented. The cost squeeze was real, the margins were thin, and the math behind a significant price increase is straightforward to follow. What the explanation does not fully answer is why the increases landed where they did — and whether holding margin was all that was happening.

Start with the structure of the cost base itself. In one restaurant sample studied by researchers, labor accounted for 36% of total operating costs, and minimum-wage costs specifically were estimated at between 4% and 10% of total costs. That's the foundation the labor argument is built on. And when you run the wage-increase numbers through it, the math produces something much smaller than the price increases customers actually saw.

A Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago study found that for every 1% increase in the minimum wage, fast-food prices rose about 0.139%. A separate study tracking fast-food chains directly found that a one-dollar minimum wage increase raised average menu prices by roughly seven cents. Seven cents on a twelve-dollar meal. That's a pass-through elasticity of about 0.13 — not nothing, but far from enough on its own to account for prices rising more than 60% at some chains over a decade.

The Berkeley research complicates the picture further without resolving it cleanly. One Berkeley IRLE paper estimated that consumers bore about 50% of higher labor costs through prices in a study of a $20 minimum wage. A separate NBER study found food-away-from-home prices in California's four in-sample metropolitan areas rose 3.3% to 3.6% relative to 17 control areas through December 2024. These studies use different methods and different comparison groups, so they are not two readings of the same variable. In the Berkeley estimate, the other half of higher labor costs never reached the menu board.

Pull all of that together and the arithmetic becomes hard to ignore. If labor is 30% to 36% of costs, and the empirical pass-through on wage increases runs somewhere around half, then labor costs — even rising sharply — produce a fraction of what actually appeared on the menu board. But the gap between what labor and commodity pressures justify and what prices actually did is where the story stops being simple.

That gap turns out to have a second dimension that the sticker price alone never shows you.

While chains were raising what you paid, some were simultaneously reducing what you got. Restaurants shrank portion sizes on certain menu items while raising prices at the same time — a double adjustment that works in the same direction twice. The sticker goes up. The serving comes down. The effective price per unit of food moves more than either change suggests on its own. The Harris Poll found that 35% of quick-service restaurant customers said they had noticed shrinkflation at QSRs over the prior year.

The timing of all of this matters. Menu prices were at their highest in over forty years, with limited-service and full-service restaurants raising prices by at least 7% over the past year. That is the environment in which portion reductions happened: alongside the cost pressure.

In 2023, 82% of operators raised menu prices, and 61% were planning to raise them again in 2024.

The limited-service CPI rose 26% from 2019 to 2024, against about 21% cumulative headline CPI inflation over the same span. Costs moved. Prices moved further. And the plans for further increases were already in place.

What the industry may not have fully priced in was that consumers were running the same arithmetic — and reaching a different conclusion.

By 2024, 62% of respondents in LendingTree-related reporting said they were eating less fast food specifically because of what it cost. That is not a rounding error in consumer sentiment. And 78% of those respondents had reclassified the experience entirely, not a quick, cheap meal, but a luxury. The word matters. Luxuries are things you cut when money gets tight. Fast food built its entire business model on being the thing you kept.

The Farmdoc Daily survey sharpens the picture further. More than half of consumers, 51.6%, said rising prices were causing them to go to fast-food restaurants less often. Price tolerance erodes much faster once customers decide a price crossed a line they can name.

The Harris Poll shows where many consumers draw the line. Nearly half of U.S. adults said a fair price for a full quick-service meal runs between five and just under ten dollars. The combos had already pushed past that range. When 75% of consumers told surveyors that cooking at home was now more economical, they weren't describing a preference. They were describing a calculation they had already made and a habit they had already changed.

Costs rose. Prices rose further. And then customers started cutting back.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts a number on what consumers were already feeling in their wallets. Real average hourly earnings decreased 0.2% from July 2025 to July 2026, and over the broader post-2019 stretch real wages were roughly flat. The category that had long served as the fallback option — the meal you kept when everything else got cut — outran both overall inflation and the paychecks of many of the people it depended on.

Numerator's tracking makes the longer arc even starker. Quick-service restaurant prices climbed 53.9% since January 2018, against a 33.2% rise in the overall consumer basket over the same period. That is not a close race. The category repriced itself at a fundamentally different rate than the economy around it, and did so across years, not in a single emergency.

With only about half of cost increases reaching the menu board, the rest was absorbed elsewhere in the business. That absorption is real, and it is not free. For an operator running on a margin that thin, a cost shock of any size is existential arithmetic.

But here is where the data stops being a cost story and starts being something harder to categorize. If roughly half of cost increases passed through to prices, and costs themselves rose sharply, then the 26% limited-service CPI increase from 2019 to 2024 has only a partial cost-based explanation — the arithmetic does not close on costs alone. Prices continued rising even as overall inflation moderated, outpacing grocery prices, while the industry pointed to costs as the driver.

That is the gap the data leaves open. Not invented, not assumed — just there, in the distance between what cost pass-through justifies and what the BLS actually recorded.

You felt it the moment you pulled up to the window. Same restaurant. The number on the screen no longer matched the category you thought you were buying from. That was not confusion. In 2014 that combo cost under six dollars, by 2024 about twelve, and rising costs explain only part of the difference.
